title: Adjoint-State Identifiability of Piezo-Tunable Valley Splitting in 2D Magnetic Heterostructures
abstract: Controlling valley degrees of freedom with mechanical strain is a promising approach for solid-state information processing. Current theoretical literature routinely predicts strain-tuned valley splitting at the microscopic level but rarely evaluates whether these quantum predictions remain statistically recoverable in realistic macroscopic devices. This manuscript establishes a fully classical, partial differential equation-constrained multiscale inverse framework for quantifying the device-level identifiability of predicted strain-tunable valley effects in two-dimensional magnetic heterostructures, demonstrated here for a molybdenum disulfide and chromium tribromide heterostructure. First-principles structural relaxations confirm a chiral $C_3$ point-group symmetry which mathematically reduces the relevant exchange-strain coupling tensor to a single scalar. A partial differential equation-constrained adjoint-state architecture successfully bridges continuum elastodynamics to valley-resolved anomalous Hall transport. Density functional theory yields a coupling estimate of $η\approx -0.07$ meV whose 95% confidence interval is consistent with zero. Evaluating this specific coupling magnitude against established thermal noise and velocity saturation limits defines a safe operating window bounded between 262.0 and 22,337.6 V/cm. Rather than asserting a confirmed nonzero material property this bounded operational window functions as a precise diagnostic threshold. Deploying this rigorous statistical identifiability framework provides a necessary mathematical filter to determine the true experimental viability of theoretically predicted two-dimensional materials before complex physical fabrication.
summary: This work develops a sophisticated, multiscale adjoint-state framework to test if theoretically predicted strain-tunable valley splitting in 2D magnetic heterostructures is actually measurable in a real device. By treating the coupling constant as an unknown parameter in an inverse problem, the authors provide a precise diagnostic threshold rather than a definitive material claim. This methodology offers a vital mathematical filter for advancing 2D materials research.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of determining the device-level identifiability of theoretically predicted strain-tunable valley splitting in 2D magnetic heterostructures.
main_result: The authors established a rigorous adjoint-state framework that provides a quantitative, statistically robust diagnostic threshold (an operational window) to assess the experimental viability of predicted quantum effects.
method: A multiscale inverse framework was developed, combining first-principles calculations, continuum elastodynamics, and a partial differential equation-constrained adjoint-state method to map microscopic parameters to macroscopic transport observables.
model_or_system: The system is a $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{CrBr}_3$ 2D magnetic heterostructure. The model incorporates a valley Hamiltonian, piezoelectric coupling ($\eta$), and is solved using a combination of DFT, continuum mechanics, and drift-diffusion transport equations.
key_observables: The transverse Hall potential difference ($V_H(x)$) and the derived safe operating window ($262.0$ to $22,337.6 	ext{ V/cm}$).
important_parameters: The exchange-strain coupling constant ($\eta$), which was found to be statistically consistent with zero based on initial DFT estimates.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system relaxes into a chiral $	ext{C}_3$ symmetry, and the macroscopic simulation uses an isothermal approximation, neglecting Joule heating.
figures_summary: The notes detail the use of finite-difference solvers for both the forward and adjoint state systems, validating the gradient calculation against finite-difference references.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical necessity of the framework (bridging quantum theory to macroscopic measurement) to developing the adjoint-state PDE constraint, applying it to the specific $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{CrBr}_3$ system, and finally deriving a quantitative diagnostic threshold.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of adjoint-state methods to bridge quantum material predictions (DFT) to measurable transport quantities (Hall effect) is a powerful, generalizable computational technique for assessing experimental feasibility in condensed matter systems.
